newsitem.title: HUNGARY: ABN-AMRO HOARE GOVETT RATES EGIS AS 'SELL'.
newsitem.headline: ABN-AMRO HOARE GOVETT RATES EGIS AS 'SELL'.

text.p: ABN-AMRO Hoare Govett rated shares in Hungarian pharmaceuticals company Egis Gyogyszergyar Rt as 'sell', due to the company's reliance on volume and on the domestic market.

The rating was triggered by the 1996 earnings reports of Egis which posted an after-tax profit of 5.58 billion forints on sales of 24.69 billion forints in 1996, against a net profit of 4.84 billion on sales of 19.81 billion in 1995.
"Egis has made little progress in bringing down their cost base or becoming less reliant on the domestic market," Tommy Erdei, ABN-AMRO Hoare Govett's Budapest-based analyst said in a desknote.
Egis expects to boost its sales to around 30 billion forints in 1997 and plans to post a pre-tax profit of 6.3 billion.

In light of Egis's management's forecast for 1997, ABN-AMRO Hoare Govett lowered its previous profit forecast slightly and expects Egis to post a net profit of 6.6 billion forints compared to the previous forecast of seven billion.
"On the back of a decrease in forecast earnings for 1997, we reiterate our sell recommendation," Erdei said.
"The real declines in net income compared with strong increases for sector rival Richter suggest that investors should switch out of Egis and into Richter."
ABN-AMRO was concerned over Egis's margins and said that "margins demonstrate clearly just how much the company relies on volume."
Unlike Richter which is able to reduce expenses when volumes fall, Egis's operating margin deteriorates whenever sales are low, Erdei said.
"Egis's reliance on volume gives rise to concern over the company's medium-term future," he said, adding they expected the year's first quarter to be disappointing for Egis.
"Even though the company will benefit from the price increase, lower volumes will dampen much of the gain."
But Egis's reliance on the domestic market was also a reason for concern, the analyst said.

In Richter's case exports account for about two-thirds of total sales, while in Egis's case domestic sales in 1996 accounted for 54.9 percent and Egis expects this ratio to fall below 50 percent in 1998.
